current_episode.title: S01 EP5 - Using AI as a change-comms wingman, with Ana-Maria Thijssen

guest.entreprise: Undisclosed (large global corporation running an SAP IT transformation programme)
guest.bio_context: Ana-Maria Thijssen joined her current change communications role approximately a year and a half after the SAP IT transformation programme had already started, meaning she had to onboard rapidly with no formal induction. She works as the sole communications professional embedded within an Organizational Change Management (OCM) team, operating across a global, multi-wave programme that spans dozens of locations worldwide. Her colleagues on the programme have been involved since January 2015, making them a key source of institutional knowledge she relies on alongside AI tools.

context.real_quote: AI became my virtual colleague. It's not a person that does my job. It's more like an entity that helps me bounce ideas and not feel so alone.
key_stats: 6,000 people surveyed across the US, the UK, and Australia in the bot-sitting study cited in this episode
69% of workers now admit to 'bot sitting' according to the study cited
Employees waste an average of 6.4 hours per week on feeding missing context and debugging AI errors, per the cited study
Ana-Maria Thijssen's SAP transformation programme will ultimately impact 6,000 users within her company
Thijssen joined the programme approximately 1.5 years after it had already started (programme launched from January 2015)
The next wave of the programme will cover 30 locations worldwide, compared to 3 locations in the first waves

pending_qa.q: What approach does Ana-Maria Thijssen recommend for prompting AI to find reliable external research and case studies?
pending_qa.r: Thijssen insists on always asking AI to provide references alongside every idea it generates — not in a single list at the end, but paired with each paragraph — so she can verify each source individually. She specifically recommends requesting academic research rather than general research, targeting sources such as peer-reviewed journals or publications like Harvard Business Review, and manually checking that every cited link actually exists and leads to a real, substantive source.

pending_qa.q: What are the risks of relying on AI-generated references in change communications work, and how can practitioners mitigate them?
pending_qa.r: Ana-Maria Thijssen warns that AI frequently produces dead links, fabricated references, or citations that lead only to blog posts reflecting one person's unverified opinion. Her mitigation strategy is to check every reference manually — confirming the website, magazine, or academic paper actually exists — and to ask specifically for academic research to raise the baseline quality of sources returned.

pending_qa.q: How is Ana-Maria Thijssen's team preparing to scale change communications across 30 locations in the next wave of their SAP programme?
pending_qa.r: With the next wave covering 30 locations across Europe and America — compared to just three locations in earlier waves — Thijssen's team is focusing on building a structured repository of training materials and templates so that local change coordinators can onboard and operate independently. The goal is for the central global team and local teams alike to be proactive rather than reactive, staying several weeks ahead of the programme timeline by ensuring everyone has access to a consistent narrative and knows where to find the materials they need.

pending_qa.q: What is the emotional value of AI for solo internal communications professionals, according to Ana-Maria Thijssen?
pending_qa.r: Thijssen identifies emotional support as one of the most significant, if unexpected, benefits of using AI: when working alone, self-doubt and professional isolation can become real obstacles, and having an AI to check ideas against or verify approaches with removes that sense of being completely on one's own. She is clear that AI does not replace human colleagues, but it does mean that a lone communicator no longer has to sit with uncertainty when no colleague is immediately available.

pending_qa.q: Will AI replace internal communications professionals, according to Ana-Maria Thijssen?
pending_qa.r: Thijssen is unequivocal that AI will not take communications jobs, arguing that AI lacks the human experience, organisational context, and people-centred judgment that practitioners bring to their roles. She acknowledges hearing this concern repeatedly over the past two years but maintains that AI is simply not human, and that the lived, contextual knowledge professionals hold within their specific organisations is something AI cannot replicate.

pending_qa.q: What is 'bot sitting' and how widespread is it among workers using AI tools in 2024–2025?
pending_qa.r: According to a study cited in the episode — surveying 6,000 people across the US, the UK, and Australia — 'bot sitting' refers to the time workers spend checking AI outputs, feeding missing context, and debugging errors rather than benefiting from efficiency gains. The study found that 69% of workers now admit to bot sitting, and that employees waste an average of 6.4 hours per week on these tasks.
